description: Somos LUNAVI, un equipo multidisciplinario que busca investigar e identificar entornos terrestres que compartan características geológicas, ambientales o topográficas con la Luna y Marte, utilizando datos abiertos de la NASA y otras agencias espaciales. Creemos que la ciencia, la colaboración y la curiosidad pueden abrir nuevas formas de comprender otros mundos.
summary:
Before every mission to the Moon or Mars, rovers, habitats and instruments are tested in places on Earth that resemble the target. Yet there is no global map of these analogs and no common way to measure similarity: catalogs are scattered, and Europe’s analog network, which gave 293 researchers 2,077 field days, closed in 2024.

LUNAVI fills that gap. It compares all 88,148 land cells on Earth with any site on the Moon or Mars, for a specific purpose: landing, habitat, rover, ice or dust. It scores 9 variables from NASA missions, cites a source for every value, and flags whether you can actually go, using 53 legal zones and 230 environmental notes.

It works: it ranks the sites agencies already chose near the top, with Apollo’s Cinder Lake in the top 0.5% for a Jezero landing and ISRO’s Ladakh in the top 0.2% for a lunar base, while rainforests and croplands score 0. It also rediscovered 3 published analogs and proposes 13 new regions.

LUNAVI serves mission teams, agencies, universities and technology testers worldwide, including regions without their own analog program, as a first filter that shows where to look first.
details:
LUNAVI tells teams where on Earth to rehearse a Moon or Mars mission, with evidence, and whether they can actually go. A user picks any point on the Moon or Mars, or a preset such as Shackleton ridge, Arcadia Planitia or Jezero crater, and a purpose: landing, habitat, rover mobility, ice or dust. LUNAVI scores all 88,148 land cells on Earth from 0 to 100, with a confidence level, a source for every value and an access label: do not travel, restricted or permit needed.

How it works: each half-degree cell on Earth gets 9 values: slope, roughness and elevation from elevation maps, temperatures and precipitation from NASA POWER, day-night temperature and vegetation from MODIS, and rock type from a global lithology map. The Moon or Mars site gets the same values, measured the same way: terrain from LOLA or MOLA at the same 500 m scale, temperature from Diviner or the Mars Climate Database, and rock type from rules over mapped data. Each value is placed on Earth's own range, similarity is 1 minus the difference, and the score is a weighted average set by purpose: a landing weighs slope and roughness most, an ice search weighs temperature. Green places score 0, and values beyond anything on Earth are flagged and left out instead of forced into a match. Legal zones and environmental notes are labels that never change the score. The best 1% of cells more than 500 km from any known analog become new findings.

Users can also ask in plain language, such as "places in Africa like Valles Marineris but colder". The Google Gemini API turns the question into filters and a short summary. Place names come from the official IAU list, so the AI never sets coordinates or changes a score.

This lets mission teams, agencies, universities and testers anywhere, including regions without their own analog program, shortlist sites in minutes and see what matters on the ground, from 56 sourced legal zones to 220 environmental notes on permits, seasons and fragile terrain. Choosing an analog has no common measure today, and Europe's funded analog field program ended in 2024; LUNAVI makes that choice reproducible and open. Next we will add real-time and socioeconomic layers and an open API.

We built it with Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, rasterio), React, TypeScript and Leaflet on a free cloud server. It needs no special hardware and runs in any browser.

We cared most about validity and honesty. LUNAVI ranks Apollo's Cinder Lake in the top 0.5% for a Jezero landing and ISRO's Ladakh in the top 0.2% for a lunar base, places 5 of 9 published analogs in its top 20%, and scores rainforests at 0; desert controls still need tuning. It is a first filter, not proof: of its 13 new findings, it flags the 7 in do-not-travel zones instead of hiding them and points to reachable ones, such as Harrat Rahat and the Mongolian Altai.
